ω = dθ/dt and α = dω/dt; integrate α(t) to find ω and θ.
Students differentiate an angle given in degrees and treat the result as radians per second.

Rotational Kinematics handled spinning with constant angular acceleration. Everything you did in Velocity and Position from Acceleration carries over to rotation with one change of letters: $x \to \theta$, $v \to \omega$, $a \to \alpha$.

$$\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}, \qquad \alpha = \dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2\theta}{dt^2}, \qquad \omega(t) = \omega_0 + \int_0^t \alpha\,dt'.$$ Angles in radians, $\omega$ in rad/s, $\alpha$ in rad/s². Every point of a rigid body shares the same $\theta$, $\omega$ and $\alpha$.

A radian is defined as arc length divided by radius, $\theta = s/r$, so it is a pure number and $s = r\theta$ holds exactly. Differentiating gives $v = r\omega$ and $a_t = r\alpha$ for a point at distance $r$ from the axis. Those simple links, and the formulas for rotational energy and work built on them, only hold with angles measured in radians.
Points at different radii share one $\theta$ and one $\omega$, but their speeds $v = r\omega$ differ.
A turntable's angle is $\theta(t) = 2t^3 - 3t^2$ (rad, s). Find $\omega$ and $\alpha$ at $t = 2\ \text{s}$.
Differentiate the angle
$\omega = 12\ \text{rad/s}$, $\alpha = 18\ \text{rad/s}^2$.
$\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt} = 6t^2 - 6t$, so $\omega(2) = 24 - 12 = 12\ \text{rad/s}$.
$\alpha = \dfrac{d\omega}{dt} = 12t - 6$, so $\alpha(2) = 18\ \text{rad/s}^2$.
A wheel spinning at $3\ \text{rad/s}$ has $\alpha(t) = 4 - 2t$ (rad/s², s). Find $\omega$ and the angle turned at $t = 3\ \text{s}$.
Integrate the angular acceleration
$\omega = 6\ \text{rad/s}$; $\theta = 18\ \text{rad}$.
$\omega(t) = 3 + \int_0^t (4 - 2t')\,dt' = 3 + 4t - t^2$, so $\omega(3) = 6\ \text{rad/s}$.
$\theta(t) = \int_0^t \omega\,dt' = 3t + 2t^2 - \tfrac{1}{3}t^3$, so $\theta(3) = 9 + 18 - 9 = 18\ \text{rad}$, almost 3 turns.

Differentiating an angle given in degrees and calling the result rad/s. If $\theta = 30t^2$ degrees, then at $t = 2\ \text{s}$, $d\theta/dt = 120$ degrees per second, which is $120 \times \pi/180 = 2.09\ \text{rad/s}$, not 120 rad/s. Check: before using $v = r\omega$, $K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$ or $P = \tau\omega$, make sure the angle was in radians; multiply degrees by $\pi/180$ and revolutions by $2\pi$.
Every kinematics method has a rotational twin.

Angular velocity is really a vector, $\vec{\omega}$, pointing along the axis: curl the fingers of your right hand the way the object turns, and your thumb points along $\vec{\omega}$. In fixed-axis problems we keep just its sign, but the vector form is what makes Torque as a Cross Product and Gyroscopes and Precession work.
Revolutions per minute (rpm) are common on motors: $1\ \text{rpm} = \dfrac{2\pi}{60}\ \text{rad/s} \approx 0.105\ \text{rad/s}$.
